The newborn's first weeks: The first weeks are a time of feeding, sleep and getting used to each other; weight loss and frequent waking are usually normal.
Newborns can lose about 7–10% of their birth weight in the first days; most regain it within 10–14 days.
Feeding 8–12 times a day and sleeping 16–18 hours are normal at this stage.
The dark green-black poo of the first days (meconium) turns yellow within a few days.
A heel-prick screening and a hearing screening are done in the first week after birth.
Track wet nappies: from day 5 on, expect at least 6 wet nappies a day.
Don't miss the first check-up after birth (usually on day 3–5).
Limit visitors; hands should be washed before touching the baby.
Ask for help so you can rest; rest while your baby sleeps.
Reluctance to feed, constant sleepiness or being impossible to wake.
Jaundice that starts in the first 24 hours, or jaundice that spreads to the palms and soles.
Fever (armpit 37.5 °C or above) or a very low body temperature: an emergency in a baby under 3 months.
Fast or difficult breathing, turning blue.
A safe sleep environment is the most effective way to reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).
Put your baby on their back for every sleep; side or tummy sleeping is not recommended.
The mattress should be firm and flat, with no pillows, duvets, soft toys or cot bumpers.
For the first 6 months, babies should sleep in the same room as their parents but in their own bed.

Keep the room at around 20–22 °C; don't overdress your baby.
A baby sleeping bag stops covers from slipping.
Avoid falling asleep with your baby on a sofa or armchair.
A dummy can be given at sleep time; it is best started once breastfeeding is established (usually weeks 3–4).

Sleep patterns in babies
Day–night rhythm develops in the first months; sleep patterns settle over time with consistent routines.
0–3 months: 14–17 hours a day, in short blocks, is normal.
4–12 months: 12–16 hours a day (including naps); night waking may continue.
Around 4 months sleep patterns can change and waking may temporarily increase.
Teething, illness and developmental leaps can disturb sleep.
Keep days bright and active and nights dim and calm.
Create a short routine done in the same order every evening, such as bath, feed and lullaby.
Try putting your baby down drowsy but awake.
Keep sleep records in the app to spot patterns.
Excessive sleepiness, not waking to feed.
Pauses in breathing during sleep, loud snoring.
If sleep problems seriously affect your family's daily life, talk to your paediatrician.
Crying and colic
Crying is how babies communicate; colic is long periods of inconsolable crying in a healthy baby.
Colic usually starts at around 2 weeks, peaks around 6 weeks and mostly passes by 3–4 months.
It often happens in the evening, as crying for more than 3 hours a day.
Hunger, wind, nappy, tiredness, being too hot/cold and wanting to be held are the most common causes.
Never shake a baby: shaken baby syndrome can cause permanent brain damage.
Check basic needs in turn: hunger, nappy, burping, temperature.
You can try gentle rocking, white noise, swaddle-like wrapping or skin-to-skin contact.
Massage the tummy gently clockwise while your baby is calm.
When you feel overwhelmed, put your baby safely in their cot, step away for a few minutes and ask for help.
If crying comes with fever, vomiting, diarrhoea, bloody stools or refusing to feed.
If the crying is high-pitched, constant and different from usual.
If weight gain is poor or you feel you can't cope.
Wind and burping
Air swallowed during feeds can cause discomfort; regular burping helps your baby feel better.
Bottle-fed babies may swallow more air.
With wind pain, babies may pull their legs up to their tummy and go red.
Mild spitting up is normal in most babies.
Halfway through and at the end of a feed, hold your baby upright on your shoulder and rub their back.
When bottle feeding, tilt the bottle so the teat stays full of milk.
Bicycle leg movements and tummy massage can help.
Supervised tummy time while awake also helps.
Repeated projectile vomiting (especially at 2–8 weeks).
A swollen tummy, green vomit or bloody stools.
Not gaining weight.
Spitting up (reflux)
Bringing up small amounts of milk after feeds is very common in the first months and usually harmless.
It happens in more than half of babies; most grow out of it by 12 months.
If your baby is happy, gaining weight and breathing comfortably, treatment is usually not needed.
Spitting up is different from vomiting: vomiting is forceful and larger in amount.
Feed more often but in smaller amounts.
Keep your baby upright for 20–30 minutes after feeds.
Avoid tight nappies and clothes.
Still put your baby on their back to sleep; raising the head of the bed or using a pillow is not recommended.
Vomit that is green, bloody or looks like coffee grounds.
Projectile vomiting, weight loss or refusing to feed.
Coughing, choking or difficulty breathing during feeds.
Fever in babies
Fever is the body's way of fighting infection, but your baby's age and general condition decide what to do.
Armpit 37.5 °C or rectal 38 °C and above counts as fever.
Any fever in a baby under 3 months (armpit 37.5 °C, rectal 38 °C and above) always needs urgent assessment.
Your baby's general condition (playing, feeding, alertness) matters more than how high the fever is.
Aspirin must not be given to children.
Dress your baby lightly, keep the room cool and breastfeed or give fluids often.
Always ask a doctor before giving a fever reducer; the dose depends on weight and the product label must be followed.
Note the temperature and any medicine given, with times.
Sponging with cold water, alcohol or vinegar is not recommended.
Any fever in a baby under 3 months.
Seizure, turning blue, a rash that doesn't fade when pressed, stiff neck, extreme weakness: call your local emergency number.
No wet nappies, dry mouth, crying without tears (dehydration).
If the fever lasts longer than 24 hours (under 2 years).
Newborn jaundice
Most newborns develop yellowish skin in the first days; it is usually harmless but needs monitoring.
Physiological jaundice usually starts on day 2–3 and clears within 1–2 weeks.
Jaundice can last a little longer in breastfed babies.
Very high jaundice levels can be harmful if untreated, so check-ups are important.
Feed often (8–12 times a day); good feeding helps clear jaundice.
Don't miss check-ups after birth.
Putting your baby in direct sunlight is not a substitute for treatment.
Jaundice that starts in the first 24 hours.
Jaundice spreading below the chest, to the palms and soles.
Your baby being very sleepy, not feeding, pale (whitish) poo or dark urine.
If jaundice lasts more than 2 weeks (3 weeks in premature babies).
Umbilical cord care
The cord stump usually dries and falls off within 1–3 weeks; keeping it clean and dry is enough.
As it dries, the cord darkens and falls off on its own.
A little bloody spotting for a few days after it falls off is possible.
Applying alcohol or other substances is usually unnecessary.
Keep the cord dry and uncovered; fold the nappy below the belly button.
If it gets dirty, clean it with lukewarm water and dry it well.
Until the cord falls off, give sponge baths instead of immersing in a tub.
Redness spreading to the surrounding skin, swelling, foul-smelling discharge.
Changes at the belly button together with fever.
If the cord hasn't fallen off by 3 weeks or the belly button keeps bleeding.
Bathing your baby
Babies don't need a bath every day; 2–3 baths a week are enough for most.
Sponge baths are enough until the cord falls off.
Bath water should be around 36–37 °C; check it with your elbow.
A baby can drown in just a few centimetres of water.
Prepare everything in advance; never leave your baby alone in the bath, even for a moment.
Use gentle, fragrance-free products suitable for babies.
Dry skin folds well after the bath.
Making the bath part of the evening routine can help with sleep.
Widespread redness, weeping or crusting of the skin.
Difficulty breathing or turning blue after the bath.
Nappy rash and nappy care
Nappy rash is redness from moisture and friction in the nappy area; with the right care it usually clears in a few days.
Leaving wet or dirty nappies on too long is the most common cause.
Nappy rash becomes more common during diarrhoea and antibiotic use.
A bright red rash spreading into skin folds with small dots at the edges may be fungal.
Change nappies often (8–12 times a day in newborns).
Clean the area with lukewarm water and pat dry without rubbing; let it air without a nappy for a while if possible.
A thin layer of zinc oxide barrier cream can be applied.
Avoid scented wet wipes.
If the rash doesn't improve in 3 days or gets worse.
Weeping sores, blisters, pus or fever.
Baby skin and rashes
Harmless changes such as spots, dry peeling and tiny white dots are common in newborn skin.
Newborn acne and milia (white dots) usually clear on their own within weeks.
Cradle cap (yellow crusting on the scalp) is common and harmless.
Eczema appears as dry, itchy, red patches and may come back.
Use lukewarm water and a small amount of baby cleanser; keep baths short.
For eczema, apply a fragrance-free moisturiser right after the bath.
For cradle cap, gently moisturise the scalp and comb with a soft brush.
Choose loose cotton clothes.
A rash that doesn't fade when pressed (doesn't disappear in the glass test): emergency.
A rash spreading with fever, or fluid-filled blisters.
Oozing, crusting or intense itching with eczema.
Teething and oral care
The first teeth usually appear around 6 months; fussiness and more drooling may happen.
Teething time varies from baby to baby; anywhere between 4 and 15 months is normal.
More drooling, a wish to chew and mild fussiness may occur.
Teething does not cause high fever or diarrhoea; these symptoms suggest another cause.
Give a clean, chilled (not frozen) teething ring.
You can gently rub the gums with a clean finger.
From the first tooth, brush twice a day with a rice-grain-sized smear of fluoride toothpaste.
Don't put your baby to sleep with a bottle; don't give sugary drinks.
Fever above 38 °C, diarrhoea or refusing to feed.
If no teeth have come through by 12 months, talk to your paediatrician.
A first dental visit is recommended after the first tooth or at 1 year.
Development: 0–6 months
In the first six months babies learn to hold up their head, smile, follow sounds and roll over.
2 months: social smile, reacting to sounds, watching faces.
4 months: holding the head steady, reaching for objects, laughing.
6 months: rolling over, sitting with support, starting to respond to their name.
Every baby develops at their own pace; differences of a few weeks are normal.
Give supervised tummy time a few times a day while awake.
Talk to your baby, sing lullabies, respond to their facial expressions.
Offer high-contrast pictures and safe, large toys.
Don't miss developmental check-ups.
Not smiling or not reacting to sounds at 2 months.
Not holding up the head or not following objects with the eyes at 4 months.
Making no sounds at all, or using one side of the body clearly less at 6 months.
Loss of a skill already gained (at any age).
Development: 6–12 months
In this period babies sit, crawl, pull to stand and make their first meaningful sounds.
9 months: sitting without support, crawling, syllables like "ba-ba", "ma-ma", stranger anxiety.
12 months: cruising along furniture, waving, pointing, 1–2 meaningful words.
Object permanence develops: they look for a hidden toy.
Make your home safe for a crawling baby.
Play back-and-forth games like peekaboo and clapping; look at picture books together.
Respond to your baby's sounds and gestures; name objects.
Don't use a baby walker: it increases the risk of falls and injuries.
Not sitting without support or making no syllables at 9 months.
No gestures such as pointing or waving at 12 months.
Not making eye contact, not responding to their name.
Loss of skills already gained.
Solid foods are started around 6 months when the baby is ready; breast milk remains the main food until 1 year.
Signs of readiness: sitting upright with support, holding the head steady, interest in food, a weaker tongue-thrust reflex.
Iron-rich foods (meat, egg yolk, lentils) are important early on.
Before 12 months, no honey, salt or sugar is added, and cow's milk is not given as the main drink.
Allergenic foods (such as egg and peanut butter) can be introduced early in a suitable texture; if there is a risk, ask a doctor.
Introduce new foods one at a time, a few days apart, and note any reactions.
Start with purées and progress with age to lumpy textures and finger foods.
Feed your baby sitting upright and under supervision.

Rash, swelling of the lips/tongue, vomiting or shortness of breath: allergy, may be an emergency.
Constant gagging, difficulty swallowing or not gaining weight.
Not moving on to lumpy foods at all by 9 months.
Formula feeding and bottle hygiene
When breast milk isn't possible or isn't enough, formula is a safe alternative; the preparation rules must be followed.
Formula must be made up with the scoop and water ratio on the pack; diluting or concentrating it is harmful.
